newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Transport sector seen driving aluminium demand.
newsitem.headline: Transport sector seen driving aluminium demand.

text.p: Strong demand for new and high-tech use of aluminium in cars, planes and boats will fuel market growth, the European Aluminium Association said on Tuesday.

The association, which represents 15 countries, said that transport was the most important market outlet with Western World demand expected to increase by four percent in 1997 and Europe to recover from a fall last year.
"It's clear that the recession in European aluminium consumption is over," Bernard Legrand, the association's chairman, told a news conference.
Legrand, who is also head of Pechiney's aluminium division, noted that London Metal Exchange (LME) inventories had fallen dramatically this year.

But he cautioned that although stocks are around 250,000 tonnes lower at about 700,000 tonnes, it was unclear how long this trend would continue and to what extent it was based on economic growth rather than industrial restocking.

Aluminium's energy-saving and environmentally-friendly properties were making it increasingly attractive to the European motor industry which could double consumption to two million tonnes within 10 years, according to the association.
In Germany, where an average 65 kg of aluminium is used in each passenger car, more than one billion litres of fuel has been saved.
Longer term forecasts show that if 200 kg of aluminium is used per car than carbon dioxide emissions could be cut by 18 million tonnes annually.

Since Audi launched the first all-aluminium car, Legrand said an increasing number of manufacturers were using aluminium in car components, such as in motor blocks and wheels. Aluminium has almost completely replaced copper in radiators.
The association saw great potential for using aluminium in car air conditioners which are becoming popular in Europe due to warmer climatic trends.
But consumer sources said that they are expensive to run.
At present aluminium is mainly used in luxury or sports cars but the light metal is expected to be used more widely in standard cars as pressure mounts to reduce emissions.
But industry sources said that volatile aluminium prices made car manufacturers cautious about making long term investments in new production lines.
Nearly all the aluminium used in car frames, doors and other parts can be recycled profitably due to its high scrap value.

In the aeronautics industry, forecasts show that growth in air traffic is expected to boost demand for aluminium in aircraft construction. Aluminium alloys, with improved metal fatigue properties, were preferred to conventional materials.
Deliveries of commercial aircraft are expected to double to 800 over the next four years.
In the maritime sector, large high speed ferries are making greater use of aluminium. The light metal with strong resistance to salt water corrosion was increasingly replacing steel.
The number of high speed ferries constructed annually is expected to rise to 50 within eight years, from 10 at present.
